Arcturus
ärk-tū´rŭs
n. (a star or constellation of the northern sky, named twice in Job; Hebrew ash, ayish)
Greek Arktouros, the bear-watcher. The KJV uses it for Hebrew ash and ayish, spoken of in Job 38 as having “sons” — a group of stars guided together as a company.

Biblical Definition

Arcturus stands in both of Job's star-lists. In the first, Job himself confesses the LORD as the one “which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south” (Job 9:9), adding that He “doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number” (Job 9:10). In the second, the LORD turns Job's own confession into an examination: “Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” (Job 38:32), and immediately after, “Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?” (Job 38:33). The stars are governed, and Job is not the governor.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Arcturus as a fixed star of the first magnitude in the constellation Bootes, whose name signifies the bear-keeper.

expand to see more

ARCTURUS, n. A fixed star of the first magnitude, in the constellation Bootes. Its name signifies the bear-keeper, from its situation behind the tail of the great bear.

ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.

Key Scripture

Job 9:9 — "Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south."

Job 9:10 — "Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number."

Job 38:32 — "Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?"

Job 38:33 — "Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?"

Modern Corruption

The whirlwind speech answers Job's suffering with astronomy, and the answer is a Person rather than an explanation.

expand to see more

Job asked why. God answered with the sea, the snow, the stars, the wild goats and the war horse, and never once addressed the question directly. That is not evasion; it is the deepest possible answer. Job's trouble was that he could not see a government behind his pain, and God's reply was to walk him through a universe of governed things — Mazzaroth brought forth in his season, Arcturus guided with his sons, the ordinances of heaven set and kept. If the constellations are led about like a flock, the sufferer is not adrift. Job's repentance in chapter 42 is not the discovery of a reason but the sight of a Ruler.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the biblical answer to affliction is the character and government of God rather than an account of causes. Two failures crowd in on this. One demands the reason and will not worship without it, which is Job's error before chapter 42. The other invents reasons on God's behalf and hands them to sufferers, which is the error of Job's friends, whom God rebuked. The book ends with the friends needing Job's prayer, and with Job saying he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear but now his eye seeth Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ash / ayish (H5906), Arcturus with his sons; mazzaroth (H4216), the constellations of the zodiac in their seasons; chuqqah (H2708), ordinance, statute.

expand to see more

Hebrew ayish (H5906) — Arcturus, the Bear with her sons; Job 9:9, 38:32.

Hebrew mazzaroth (H4216) — the constellations in their seasons; Job 38:32 only.

Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — ordinance, appointed statute; Job 38:33, Jeremiah 31:35.

Hebrew mishtar (H4896) — dominion, rule; Job 38:33 only.

Hebrew nachah (H5148) — to lead, guide; Job 38:32, Psalm 23:3.

Usage

"“Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades” — Job's own confession."

"“Canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” — the confession turned into a question."

"“Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven?” — the government Job could not see."
